title: Data Integrity
overview: Paper 1 asks candidates to describe and apply validation and verification techniques, and to explain how parity checks and check digits detect errors introduced during data entry and transmission. Answers score when a named check is matched to a concrete example and its limitation is stated, not just its purpose.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of the need for validation and verification techniques in data-capture and data-transfer processes.
Describe and apply validation checks, including range check, length check, type check, presence check, format check, check digit and existence/lookup check.
Describe verification methods, including visual (proofreading) checking and double data entry, and explain their limitations.
Explain how errors can be introduced during data transmission and describe the use of parity checks to detect them.
Calculate and interpret a parity bit for a set of data using even or odd parity, and calculate a simple check digit.

definitions.definition: The accuracy, consistency and reliability of data throughout its life, from entry to storage and transmission.
An automated check performed by software to ensure that data entered meets defined rules before it is accepted, without confirming the data is actually true.
A check that data entered or copied matches its original source, catching transcription errors.
An extra digit calculated from the other digits in a code and added to it, used to detect data-entry errors such as mistyped or transposed digits.
An extra bit added to a unit of data so that the total number of 1-bits is even (even parity) or odd (odd parity), letting a receiver detect single-bit transmission errors.
A value calculated from a block of transmitted data and sent with it, recalculated by the receiver to detect whether the block has changed.
An error introduced when a person copies or types data incorrectly, for example transposing two digits.

sections.title: What is data integrity?
content: Data integrity is the accuracy and consistency of data over its lifetime. It is a different concern from data security: security protects data from unauthorised access, while integrity is about whether the data itself is correct and has not been corrupted. Integrity can be threatened by human input error, hardware faults, software bugs, transmission errors on a communication line, or malicious alteration.
bullets: Data can be perfectly secure (no one unauthorised can reach it) yet still be inaccurate.
Integrity checks aim to catch errors as early as possible, ideally before data is stored or used.
No single check guarantees data is correct; several checks are normally combined.

sections.title: Validation
content: Validation is an automated check, carried out by software, that rejects data failing to meet defined rules before it can be accepted. It only confirms that a value is reasonable or plausible for its field; it cannot confirm the value is actually true. Common validation checks include a range check (a value must fall between set boundaries, for example a percentage mark between 0 and 100), a length check (the number of characters must be within set boundaries, for example a password of at least eight characters), a type check (data must be of an expected data type, for example a numeric age), a presence check (a required field must not be left empty), a format check (data must match a specified pattern, for example a date as DD/MM/YYYY), an existence or lookup check (data must match an item already held in a table or file, for example a product code that exists in a stock file), and a check digit (an extra digit calculated from the other digits in a code, described in detail below).
bullets: A value that passes every validation check can still be the wrong value for that record.
Validation rules are defined once in the software and applied automatically to every entry.
Combining several checks on one field catches more kinds of error than relying on just one.

sections.title: Verification
content: Verification checks that data entered or copied matches its original source; it catches transcription errors rather than judging whether a value is reasonable. Visual checking (proofreading) means comparing the data shown on screen or on a printout against the original document. Double data entry means the same data is entered twice, independently, often by two different people, and the two entries are compared automatically; any mismatch is flagged for a human to resolve.
bullets: Verification cannot detect an error that already exists in the original source document.
Double data entry cannot detect an error made identically by both entries, though this is unlikely by chance.
Verification and validation are complementary and are normally both used on the same data.

sections.title: Errors during data transmission
content: Data sent over a communication line can be altered by electrical interference or 'noise' on the line, causing one or more bits to be received differently from how they were sent. Because the receiver cannot see the original data to compare it directly, transmission errors must be detected using extra information sent alongside the data itself, such as a parity bit or a checksum.
bullets: Longer transmissions and noisier lines increase the chance that a bit is altered.
Detecting an error only shows that something changed; it does not by itself say which bit changed.
When an error is detected, the usual response is to request the data again.

sections.title: Parity checks
content: Before transmission, an extra parity bit is added to each unit of data so that the total number of 1-bits, including the parity bit, matches an agreed rule: even parity requires an even total, odd parity requires an odd total. The receiver recounts the 1-bits in the data it received and compares the result with the agreed parity. If the count no longer matches, at least one bit has changed and an error is flagged, usually leading to a retransmission request.
bullets: The sender and receiver must agree in advance whether even or odd parity is being used.
A single-bit error is always detected, because it always changes whether the total count is even or odd.
If exactly two bits change, the total count of 1-bits returns to what was expected, so the error is missed.

examples.label: Calculating and checking an even parity bit
examples.content:
Data to send: 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 (four 1-bits)
Even parity requires an even total, so the parity bit added = 0
Transmitted byte: 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 0 (parity bit is the last bit)

Received byte: 1 0 1 1 0 1 1 0 (one bit has changed in transit)
Receiver counts the 1-bits: five 1-bits, an odd total
Expected even parity, but the total is odd, so an error is detected
The receiver requests the data again

sections.title: Checksums
content: A checksum is calculated from an entire block of data, for example by adding together the numeric value of every byte in the block, and is transmitted along with that block. The receiver performs the same calculation on the data it received and compares its result with the transmitted checksum. A mismatch shows the block has changed during transmission. Checksums are used to check larger blocks of data, whereas a parity bit is normally used to check one small unit, such as a byte, at a time.
bullets: A checksum can be defeated by errors that cancel out, just as parity can, though this is less likely across a large block.
Checksums are common in file transfers and network protocols, protecting an entire packet or file.
Like parity, a checksum only detects that an error occurred; it does not correct it.

sections.title: Check digits
content: A check digit is an extra digit added to a code, calculated from the other digits using a fixed algorithm, and is used to detect data-entry errors such as a mistyped digit or two digits being transposed. When a code is entered or scanned, the system repeats the calculation on the digits received and compares the result with the check digit that was entered; a mismatch means the code has probably been entered incorrectly, and the record is rejected. Check digits are widely used in identifiers such as ISBNs and barcodes.
bullets: A check digit catches most single-digit and transposition errors, which are the most common typing mistakes.
A check digit cannot confirm the code refers to the correct, intended item, only that it is internally consistent.
Different code systems use different algorithms; the calculation method must be agreed in advance.

examples.label: Calculating a modulo-11 check digit for a 9-digit code
examples.content:
Code digits: 0 4 4 0 5 2 3 7 X (positions 1-9, X is the check digit to find)

Multiply each digit by its weight (position counted from the left, 10 down to 2):
0x10 + 4x9 + 4x8 + 0x7 + 5x6 + 2x5 + 3x4 + 7x3 = 0+36+32+0+30+10+12+21 = 141

Divide the total by 11 and find the remainder: 141 / 11 = 12 remainder 9
Check digit = 11 - 9 = 2

If the calculated check digit is 10, the digit X is used instead
The completed code is: 0 4 4 0 5 2 3 7 2

comparisonTable.title: Validation compared with verification
rows: Whether data meets defined rules, such as type, range or format
Whether data matches its original source
Automatically, by software, against fixed rules
By comparing two independent entries, or a person proofreading
Can it guarantee the data is correct?
No; it only rejects clearly unreasonable data
No; it cannot detect an error already in the source, or one repeated in both entries

diagram.title: Detecting an error with even parity
nodes: Sent byte: 1 0 1 1 0 0 1, parity bit 0 added (four 1-bits, even)
Received byte: 1 0 1 1 0 1 1, parity bit still 0 (five 1-bits, odd)
Recalculated parity is odd, expected even: mismatch
Receiver flags the error and requests retransmission

analysisChains.title: A single-bit transmission error caught by parity
steps: The sender calculates a parity bit so the byte has an even number of 1-bits
The byte and its parity bit are transmitted
Interference on the line flips one bit during transmission
The receiver recalculates parity and finds an odd number of 1-bits
analysisChains.evaluation: The mismatch reveals that an error occurred, but parity alone does not identify which bit changed, so the only available response is to request the data again.

analysisChains.title: Two bits flipping during the same transmission
steps: Interference flips two bits within the same byte
The total number of 1-bits changes by two, so it is still even
The receiver recalculates parity and finds it matches the expected value
The error goes undetected and the corrupted byte is accepted
analysisChains.evaluation: Simple parity is unreliable whenever an even number of bits change, which is why systems that must be highly reliable use stronger checks such as a checksum across a larger block.

analysisChains.title: A mistyped product code caught by a check digit
steps: An operator transposes two digits while typing a product code
The system recalculates the check digit from the digits that were entered
The recalculated digit does not match the check digit that was typed or scanned
The record is rejected and the operator is asked to re-enter the code
analysisChains.evaluation: Check digits catch common typing errors such as transposition efficiently, but cannot confirm that a valid-looking code refers to the correct, intended item.

examTips: State that validation checks a value is 'reasonable', not that it is correct; a valid but wrong value can still pass every check.
Name the specific validation check being used, for example 'range check, because 105 is outside 0-100', rather than saying only 'it checks the data'.
For parity questions, show the recalculation step and state clearly whether it matches, not just the final parity bit.
Distinguish verification (matches the source) from validation (meets defined rules) precisely; the two are often confused.
commonMistakes: Saying validation checks that data is 'correct', when it only checks that data is plausible against a rule.
Confusing a check digit, attached to a single code to detect key-entry errors, with a checksum, calculated from a whole block of transmitted data.
Claiming parity always detects an error, when it fails to detect an even number of bit changes.
Describing double data entry as a form of validation rather than verification.
Forgetting to state which parity is being used, even or odd, when answering a parity question.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between validation and verification?
quickRecall.answer: Validation is an automated check that data meets defined rules, such as type, range or format; verification checks that data entered or copied matches its original source.

quickRecall.question: Give two examples of validation checks.
quickRecall.answer: Any two of: range check, length check, type check, presence check, format check, check digit, existence/lookup check.

quickRecall.question: Why can validated data still be wrong?
quickRecall.answer: Validation only confirms the data is a reasonable, plausible value for its field; it cannot confirm the value is actually true or accurate.

quickRecall.question: Describe double data entry.
quickRecall.answer: The same data is entered twice, independently, and the two entries are compared automatically; a mismatch flags a possible error for a person to resolve.

quickRecall.question: What is a parity bit used for?
quickRecall.answer: An extra bit added to a unit of data so the total number of 1-bits is even or odd as agreed, letting a receiver detect single-bit transmission errors.

quickRecall.question: Why can parity fail to detect an error?
quickRecall.answer: If an even number of bits change, the total count of 1-bits is restored to the expected parity, so the error is not detected.

quickRecall.question: What is a check digit used for?
quickRecall.answer: An extra digit, calculated from the other digits in a code, added to detect data-entry errors such as mistyped or transposed digits.
